CausalChain: HCC tumor cells overexpress PD-L1 -> PD-L1 engagement with PD-1 suppresses T cell anti-tumor activity -> Oncolytic viruses selectively infect tumor cells and induce immunogenic cell death -> Engineering these viruses to carry CRISPR/Cas9 components allows targeted disruption of PD-L1 in tumor cells -> Reduced PD-L1 expression alleviates local immune suppression -> Enhanced T cell activation synergizes with immune checkpoint blockade therapy -> Improved anti-tumor response leads to tumor regression in HCC
Hypothesis: Oncolytic viral vectors engineered to deliver CRISPR/Cas9 components that disrupt the PD-L1 gene in hepatocellular carcinoma cells will reduce tumor-mediated immune suppression and, in combination with immune checkpoint inhibitors, produce a synergistic anti-tumor effect.
Abstract: We propose a novel therapeutic approach for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) that combines engineered oncolytic viral vectors with CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated gene editing to target the PD-L1 immune checkpoint. HCC tumors display a highly immunosuppressive microenvironment, partly due to the overexpression of PD-L1 which dampens T cell responses. By harnessing the tumor selectivity of oncolytic viruses and engineering them to co-deliver CRISPR/Cas9 systems designed to disrupt the PD-L1 gene, it is possible to decrease local immune evasion. This genetic reprogramming could restore immune surveillance and boost the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors. Such a combinatorial modality may synergistically activate anti-tumor T cell responses, overcome resistance to current immunotherapies, and ultimately improve patient outcomes in HCC.
